stemMd: Let $A$ be the set of the positive divisors of $12$ and let $B$ be the set of the positive divisors of $18$. How many elements does the Cartesian product $A \times (A \cap B)$ contain?
explanationMd:
The size of a Cartesian product is the **product** of the sizes of the two factors, because each element of the first set is paired with each element of the second. So find the two sets first.

**List the divisors.**

$$A = \{1,\,2,\,3,\,4,\,6,\,12\}, \qquad B = \{1,\,2,\,3,\,6,\,9,\,18\}$$

**Intersect.** The divisors common to both are $A \cap B = \{1,\,2,\,3,\,6\}$, which has $4$ elements. (These are exactly the divisors of $6$, the greatest common divisor of $12$ and $18$.)

**Multiply.** $A$ has $6$ elements, so

$$|A \times (A \cap B)| = |A| \cdot |A \cap B| = 6 \cdot 4 = 24$$

**How to check.** Picture a table with one row for each element of $A$ and one column for each element of $A \cap B$: $6$ rows and $4$ columns, so $24$ cells, each cell one ordered pair such as $(12,\,3)$.

distractorRationale.a: This is $6 + 4 = 10$: the sizes of the two sets were added. Adding counts the elements of a union of disjoint sets; a Cartesian product pairs every element of one set with every element of the other, so the sizes multiply.
distractorRationale.b: This is $4 \cdot 4 = 16$, the size of $(A \cap B) \times (A \cap B)$. The intersection was used for both factors, but the first factor is the whole of $A$.
distractorRationale.d: This is $6 \cdot 6 = 36$, the size of $A \times B$ (or $A \times A$). The second factor is the intersection $A \cap B$, which has only $4$ elements, not the whole of $B$.

accessibilityText: A is the set of positive divisors of 12 and B is the set of positive divisors of 18. The question asks how many elements are in the Cartesian product of A with the intersection of A and B. The four answer options are the whole numbers 10, 16, 24 and 36.

provenance.notes: Original item on the sets syllabus entry (intersection and Cartesian product). Divisor sets are small enough to list by hand; the distractors separate adding from multiplying and using the wrong factor.
